narrative_statement: When dermatological diagnosis learners differ by expertise level, reasoning-process instruction triggers relative reliance on analytic and similarity-based processes, leading to instructionally modifiable reasoning-process reliance.
When learners are novice diagnosticians, feature-oriented and similarity-trusting instructions trigger additive clinical reasoning, leading to improved diagnostic performance.

When novice ECG diagnosticians received the whatever-strategy-comes-naturally prompt, an incorrect diagnostic suggestion was intended to trigger greater non-analytic reliance; without spontaneous combined reasoning uptake, accuracy was lower with incorrect than correct suggestions in the no-instruction group.

When novices who had just learned diagnostic rules received the whatever-strategy-comes-naturally prompt, a counter-indicative feature prompt was intended to trigger greater analytic reliance on features, and limited spontaneous combined reasoning uptake led to lower accuracy in the no-instruction condition.

When novice ECG diagnosticians were given an incorrect diagnostic suggestion intended to induce greater non-analytic reliance, the combined analytic and non-analytic reasoning prompt was interpreted as supporting avoidance of single-mode reasoning, leading to comparatively greater accuracy in the bias-incorrect condition.

When novice ECG diagnosticians faced a counter-indicative feature prompt that biased consideration away from the correct diagnosis, the combined analytic and non-analytic reasoning prompt was interpreted as triggering maintained reasoning balance, leading to no accuracy decline under the biasing feature.

When undergraduate learners have no prior ECG experience, combined reasoning diagnostic instruction provides an instructed combined feature and familiarity strategy, triggering empowered use of multiple diagnostic strategies, leading to improved performance beyond no instructions.

When ECG diagnostic categories are similar and easily confusable, contrastive learning instruction provides Contrastive Diagnostic Scaffolding, triggering possible understanding of symptom diagnosticity and reduced premature closure from feature-overlap awareness, leading to higher diagnostic accuracy than non-contrastive learning.

When undergraduate learners have no prior ECG experience and are left unguided, free-choice reasoning prompts trigger self-selected combined reasoning with less benefit, leading to lower accuracy than explicit combined instruction.

When the delayed test includes ECGs previously seen during training, one-to-one ECG diagnostic training provides prior exposure to specific ECG exemplars, triggering inferred similarity-based recognition processes, leading to higher accuracy for old than new ECGs.

When learners face diagnostic difficulty, computer-supported case-based worked examples provide a diagnostic process schema and worked examples, triggering lower cognitive load and more cognitive resources invested in schema construction, leading to effective and efficient learning.

When learners with additive, mechanistic diagnostic habits work in complex diagnostic learning environments, erroneous examples with only KCR feedback provide right-or-wrong judgements, triggering deduction from later solution steps, superficial processing and limited deep conceptual understanding, leading to detrimental diagnostic knowledge acquisition.

When students have insufficiently integrated diagnostic schemata, computer-supported case-based worked examples provide severe erroneous examples plus elaborated GP feedback, triggering effective processing, error identification and correct-solution understanding, leading to improved diagnostic knowledge acquisition.

When arterial hypertension is part of the curriculum and assessment, a worked-example learning session provides secondary-hypertension cases and a structured diagnostic schema, triggering cognitive resources for schema construction, leading to a six-week conceptual knowledge effect and MCQ advantage.

When Year 2 medical students undertake the Integrated Cases Section course, a course designed to promote clinical reasoning is intended to activate clinical reasoning, and the course is associated with increased diagnostic reasoning confidence and improved script concordance test performance.

When medical students have an incorrect initial diagnosis, a prompt to query the initial hypothesis triggers thinking about that hypothesis, leading to allowed rectification of the incorrect diagnosis and reduced diagnostic error.
When medical students have a correct initial diagnosis, a prompt to query the initial hypothesis triggers thinking about that hypothesis, leading to no harm to the correct diagnosis.

When diagnosticians have developed expertise and encounter a cascade of data abnormalities, years of diligent study and practice support logical connection of abnormalities to disease mechanisms, leading to identification of failing organ systems.

When learners have few initial aspirations to become laboratorians, particular courses or instructors, or learners’ discovery of the diagnostic power of laboratory data, can trigger piqued interest in clinical pathology.

When students are learning clinical reasoning, a case-based clinical reasoning seminar intervention provides a focus on cognitive features of reasoning, intended to trigger insight into those reasoning features, leading to improved aspects of diagnostic competence.

When undergraduate primary care rotations are short, video-enriched VP cases provide simulated GP consultations with patient videos, triggering active virtual participation in consultations, leading to theorised enhanced acquisition of primary care clinical reasoning skills.

When VP cases are rolled out to primary care rotation cohorts as optional self-directed access, the self-directed access triggers limited voluntary engagement with cases, leading to restricted uptake among potential students.

When students are in a six-week primary care rotation, self-directed VP cases provide autonomous clip control and attempt scores, triggering formative use and progress mapping, leading to repeated use across days and higher end-of-rotation usage.

When short rotations limit longitudinal exposure, time-compressed VP case scenarios provide a compressed longitudinal patient course, triggering observation of test-of-time and test-of-treatment reasoning, leading to theorised construction of clinical reasoning skills.

When GP diagnostic approaches are not explicitly taught, tailored decision-tree VP cases provide virtual experience of these real-time reasoning strategies, triggering practice and refinement of GP reasoning, leading to theorised acquisition of primary care reasoning skills.

When clinical cases are more familiar and learners already hold well-defined illness scripts, there is reduced scope for elaboration and reconstruction, so self-explanation diagnostic case solving leads to no diagnostic performance benefit for familiar topics.

When students face less familiar clinical cases with less developed illness scripts, the opportunity to generate explanations to oneself triggers active sense-making, symptom linking, and knowledge reconstruction, leading to better delayed diagnostic performance on less familiar cases.

When third-year medical students in clerkship training generated self-explanations without feedback, the intervention provided definitions, examples, and instructions prompting self-explanation, triggering extensive case elaboration and leading to better diagnostic performance after one week.

When undergraduate clinical reasoning learners use evPaeds, it provides individual or small-group clinical reasoning practice and is positively received by students, with reported outcomes of student popularity and clinical reasoning practice/development.

When students have little prior prioritisation decision experience, shadowing where the FY1 makes decisions and the student follows triggers feeling cocooned from responsibility, leading to feeling not fully prepared for FY1 decisions.

When advanced students nearing FY1 transition feel unprepared for clinical decision making, the tool, tutorial and simulated ward scenarios trigger positive adaptation and learning, leading to increased subjective preparedness for FY1 decision making.

When students have no prior experience of multitasking situations, multiple tasks and acutely unwell patients trigger stress from pager interruption, leading to abandoned structured patient assessment.
When learners lack familiarity with AM I HERO NOW, the memorable mnemonic decision prompt triggers perceived time and complexity burden, leading to the tool not being used in simulated practice.
When students are familiar with existing structured tools, a visible SBAR referral prompt triggers reduced fear and more comfortable senior communication, leading to greater SBAR use.

When learners have underdeveloped illness scripts, an alternative-diagnosis generation prompt likely triggers only partial reflective processing, leading to less delayed learning than structured reflection and a significant immediate-to-delayed decrease within that condition.

When Year 4 students have theoretical knowledge but limited patient exposure, structured contrastive and absent-feature reflection prompts trigger elaboration and knowledge reorganisation, leading to improved illness-script quality and better delayed diagnostic transfer.

When learners have underdeveloped illness scripts, demanding step-by-step case comparison may trigger high cognitive load, exhaustion, or confusion, leading to poorer immediate diagnostic performance.

When learners have underdeveloped illness scripts, speeded single-diagnosis instruction lowers the likelihood of reflective processing, leading to no significant signs of immediate-test learning in the non-reflection conditions.
When novice learners receive schema grouping by clinical variables, the resource triggers structured rather than factual knowledge change, leading to no factual knowledge score advantage.

When cardiac auscultation novice students receive schema-based instruction, feature-based diagnostic support triggers uptake of schema features during reasoning, leading to higher diagnostic success for taught lesions.

When cardiac auscultation novice students receive schema-based distinguishing features, the resource triggers reduced incorrect feature identification, leading to higher diagnostic success for untaught diagnostic lesions.

When students face an unknown systolic murmur diagnostic task, diagnosis-specific feature tables can trigger incorrect feature identification that derails reasoning, leading to lower diagnostic accuracy relative to schema-based instruction.

When pre-clerkship novice learners receive schema-based instruction, linked and structured clinical information triggers modified structured knowledge organisation, leading to higher structured knowledge scores.

When students have prior endocrine training, a similar-case series provides variation in presentations and causes, triggering comparison of prior knowledge with case findings and other cases, leading to improved knowledge of enabling conditions and consequences.

When students have very poor, incomplete, or error-prone prior knowledge, unsupported similar-case reasoning with official diagnosis feedback only is insufficient for debugging unresolved reasoning errors, leading to hampered biomedical fault integration.

When advanced medical students near internships are given an unguided multiple-case learning task, the open diagnose-explain-and-learn instruction triggers limited overt demonstration of learning in some students, leading to doubts about their ability to exploit case learning fully.

When students have incomplete and error-prone knowledge, a similar-case series provides multiple related endocrine cases that can trigger active biomedical debugging effort, leading in some students to partial remediation of misconceptions while others ignore errors.

When advanced medical students are near internships, reduced-feedback similar-case reasoning provides multiple cases with the same underlying problem and official diagnosis feedback, triggering faster and more secure case representation, which is associated with implicit learning and strengthened concept links.

When advanced medical students near licensure diagnose OSCE standardized-patient cases, a structured analytic-reasoning table and differential-diagnosis prompt trigger consideration of alternatives and conflicting findings, leading to higher diagnostic accuracy.

When advanced medical students near licensure are in a control condition with an answer sheet lacking the analytic table, the request for one most probable diagnosis is associated with diagnosis without analytic listing processes, leading to lower accuracy relative to the analytic-reasoning group.

When a case is too complex relative to students’ medical knowledge, analytic-reasoning prompts may trigger analytic reasoning, but the knowledge–complexity mismatch constrains benefit, leading to analytic reasoning being ineffective.

When a clinical presentation is typical, students’ heuristic pattern recognition may be sufficient, so the structured analytic-reasoning table can still trigger alternative consideration but adds no diagnostic-accuracy benefit for that case.

When cases are already familiar heart failure cases, self-explanation diagnostic case solving still provides opportunities to generate explanations to oneself, but is associated with reduced engagement and elaboration relative to less familiar cases; the reported benefit was only demonstrated for unfamiliar cases.

When third-year medical students work with less familiar jaundice cases, self-explanation diagnostic case solving provides opportunities to generate explanations to oneself, triggering more extensive active thinking and greater self-explanation production, which the authors link to a positive effect on unfamiliar-case diagnosis.

When clinical cases are less familiar and sufficiently challenging, self-explanation diagnostic case solving provides opportunities to generate explanations to oneself, triggering biomedical inference generation and linking of biomedical with clinical knowledge, which may lead to a coherent disease representation and easier future diagnostic retrieval.

When students’ specific knowledge is less elaborate and they work from clinical case summaries, self-explanation diagnostic case solving provides an opportunity to generate explanations to oneself, triggering active but error-prone knowledge construction and staying closer to the case text, leading to more paraphrases and errors.

When cytology novice participants receive non-feature-driven labelled exposure and are prompted to identify helpful features, they self-identify abnormal-cell features, leading to spontaneous diagnostic criteria generation with lay descriptions resembling standard cytopathology features.

When cytology novice participants receive exhaustive feature-list reasoning and feature-based diagnostic support, this triggers careful systematic feature consideration, which is associated with no diagnostic advantage over nonanalytic training and lower efficiency.

When cytology novice participants receive nonannotated normal/abnormal image pairs and a first-impression similarity prompt, these resources trigger early nonanalytic reasoning, leading to intended nonanalytic pattern-recognition skill development, improved diagnostic performance, and more efficient responses.

When cytology novice participants are given a combined analytic/nonanalytic reasoning prompt whose meaning is not entirely clear, the instruction may trigger confusion, leading to decreased diagnostic accuracy and a significant decline in d prime.

When cytology novice participants receive annotated images, feature-based diagnostic support, and analytic feature-analysis instruction, these resources trigger feature-focused diagnostic analysis and greater readiness to report abnormalities, leading to improved discrimination and reduced miss errors.

When everyday clinical practice is constrained by patient-safety concerns, repeated serious-game practice supports repeated play and memory storage, leading to improved performance in a second gaming session.

When participants have different levels of biliary-disease expertise, realistic biliary decision cases trigger use of clinical experience in case solving, leading to decision accuracy that discriminates expertise levels.

When clinically relevant expertise groups are compared for assessment, timer-based case solving is designed to trigger intrinsic motivation under time pressure, but the measured time required to solve cases is not a valid assessment parameter.

When learners are novice medical students with little clinical experience, fixed timed case challenges with feedback can trigger frustration, leading to the level of difficulty being too high for some students.

When many surgical clinicians already have video-game experience, serious-game design for voluntary engagement triggers enjoyment, challenge, and involvement, leading to willingness to recommend the game and play in free time.

When undergraduate medical students are learning diagnostic reasoning, Casebook provides real patient EHR cases with explicit modelling of physician reasoning, triggering understanding of physician thought processes, leading to intended learning of decision-making skills.

When students have limited access to common patient presentations, Casebook’s EHR-based case-pool creation provides access to multitudes and collections of similar cases, triggering pattern recognition and illness-script development, leading to intended suitable and valid diagnoses.

When undergraduate students are learning clinical reasoning, Casebook’s progress measurement during case navigation provides decision-point questions, immediate feedback, and the real physician decision, triggering a grasp of the possible diagnostic path, leading to diagnostic reasoning being tested rather than factual knowledge alone.

When diagnostic errors have been discovered in records, viewing diagnostic-error cases provides annotated records of mistakes and consequences, triggering students to examine error causes and sequences, leading to an intended reduction in diagnostic error.

When false-positive cases had no correct second diagnosis, search-satisficing CFS training provided SSB missed-second-diagnosis teaching; oversearching occurred in both groups, leading to incorrect second diagnoses without CFS excess and no significant oversearching difference.

When analytic processing is limited by working memory and cognitive load, analytic CFS training provides an active cognitive process to counter bias, which the authors hypothesise may overwhelm cognitive load, leading to no impact on diagnostic error prevention.

When novice senior medical students received a cognitive forcing strategies seminar, the seminar provided self-monitoring and bias-countering strategy, but triggered no greater second-diagnosis search than control, leading to no significant improvement in second-diagnosis accuracy.

When novices may lack sufficient experience to employ nonanalytic reasoning, CFS training provides metacognitive bias-identification techniques, but their reliance on analytic feature-counting constrains benefit, leading to little benefit from CFS.

When availability-bias cases contained a possible common but incorrect diagnosis and an uncommon correct diagnosis, instruction provided a warning about availability bias, yet learners still identified common incorrect diagnoses, leading to no improvement in uncommon diagnosis identification.

When cases concern a less familiar clinical topic, self-explanation diagnostic case solving provides opportunities to generate explanations to oneself, triggering active thinking while self-explaining and leading to improved diagnostic accuracy and performance.
When example observation lacks active-processing prompts, listening to natural raw self-explanation examples may trigger passive listening, leading to no added value on transfer cases.

When third-year medical students observe same-level peers, peer self-explanation examples containing irrelevant details and uncorrected errors may trigger little learning from those examples, leading to no performance advantage by model type.

When students have already self-explained the same cases, listening to peer or expert self-explanation examples provides immediate feedback on reasoning, triggering critical revision of knowledge representations and leading to an immediate maintained gain in diagnostic accuracy.

When early clerkship students observe expert self-explanations, expert reasoning with skipped and abstract steps may trigger difficulty relating the reasoning to their own knowledge, leading to expert models being no more effective than peer models.

When Year 3 clerks work with less familiar jaundice cases, self-explanation diagnostic case solving provides opportunities to generate explanations to oneself, triggering knowledge elaboration and biomedical-clinical linking, leading to near-transfer diagnostic gains.

When far-transfer cases are more difficult, resident SE examples without prompts provide the same recordings but lack prompt-supported additional self-explanation; because active processing appears critical, this pathway leads to no far-transfer performance advantage over control.

When near-transfer cases are similar to the training cases, the SE-alone control condition provides case self-explanation, which the authors suggest triggers deeper processing over the week, leading to delayed rather than immediate diagnostic improvement.

When junior residents are cognitively congruent near peers, resident SE examples provide more developed but relatable reasoning, triggering students to elaborate, confirm and complete their diagnostic arguments, leading to accelerated and maintained improvement.

When resident reasoning is near-peer and cognitively congruent, resident SE examples with prompts provide relatable modelling and prompts, triggering comparison plus additional self-explanation and deep processing, leading to far-transfer diagnostic performance gains.

When Year 4 clinical medical students encounter repeated case-based learning, key-feature question prompts with spaced immediate feedback trigger storage and retrieval of knowledge, leading to higher long-term clinical reasoning scores.
When examinations are formative and no incentive is provided, assessments without credit points trigger students not to revise, contributing to disappointing overall retention performance.

When e-seminars are self-paced, additional questions in test cases trigger more time spent on test items; this has only weak association with better outcomes, and the testing effect persists after controlling for time-on-task.

When students have answered an item incorrectly on a prior test, item-level feedback and explanations of incorrect distractors trigger learning from feedback, leading some students to correct that item on a subsequent test.

When clinicians’ reasoning is automated in practice, teaching clinical reasoning provides an opportunity to review reasoning pathways, triggering reflection on their own reasoning, leading to improved diagnostic efficiency, fewer assumptions and investigations, and improved patient satisfaction.

When novice learners have limited clinical experience, teaching clinical reasoning within a consultation skill framework provides a deconstructed consultation focused on the reasoning pathway, triggering understanding of expert thinking and reasoning, leading to enhanced student clinical reasoning ability.

When a student is familiar with the clinician reasoning model, supervised performance consultation provides interjected questions when reasoning is unclear, triggering articulation of reasoning during the work-up, leading to the student being kept on track during performance.

When there is an experience gap between practising clinicians and learners, a tacit pick-up approach provides only automated reasoning on display, triggering difficulty grasping the reasoning, leading to a barrier to learning clinical reasoning.

When students have diagnostic knowledge but find patient-information navigation challenging, a coached comprehension consultation provides prompts about reasoning relevance, triggering active tracking of demonstrated reasoning, leading students to determine primary and differential diagnoses.
